To clarify, and to put a point on it, they are dying of cancer. Their death will be painful and prolonged. All they want is to simply die peacefully (with your help) and not have to face the anguish of a prolonged death or subject their loved ones to witnessing that misery. For the sake of conversation, let's put all laws aside - just you, the patient, and your decision. What do you do? What is the ethical decision?
If you're a doctor and your patient is terminal, is it ethical to assist in their suicide?

Ok, I'll take a stab at this one to usher in discussion.

The ethical decision is one made in accordance with a system that provides rules for deciding so. If we decide it is ethical to assist in the suicide then the rules offer such indication. If we condemn the act as unethical it is, once again, the rules that decide as much. The question is then, what rules do we abide by?

I am of the opinion that finding which rules to abide by is almost as impossible as discerning the rules that which truth follows.

If you are sure they will die and that their cancer is terminal I feel as if it would be up to the individual to decide. In your scenario the patient desires to die sooner rather than later. My ethics are for the most part are based off of empathy and reducing suffering. I would say that it would be unethical to not assist the patient if you are the only one who is able to do so. Letting an individual suffer because of your own inability to deal with the ethical dilemma would be cruel.

The point of contention with healthcare providers whenever this is phrased ultimately comes down to the Hippocratic oath. In this they promise to do no harm with the knowledge they have gained as healers, pretty obvious why they take umbrage with killing people. That being said the question really is: is it more harm to sit here and torture them with a painful treatment I know wont work, or to end their life. Ultimately for me it would come down to this:

  1. Do my colleagues, not just myself, feel that treatment is not going to yield any results even prolonging the patients life? This because the idea of one man, even a professional being capable of making a judgement of such gravity is, to me, absurd. Also the potential to prolong a life is also the potential to save it, there are advances every day that I can never predict.

  2. Has the patient requested it in multiple occasions, including multiple times during which they were not clearly emotional and in unusually intense suffering? The potential for a patient to be requesting this out of repeated moments of desperation is high to say the least, it's my duty as a care provider to ensure that it is not only in these moments that they feel death is truly what they desire.

  3. Does the patient truly understand their condition, the process of their euthanasia, and the aftermath of their decision? Firstly it's fairly obvious that not all patients understand exactly where they are in their disease, they must be made to understand on as deep a level possible. Next, euthanasia is not guaranteed to be painless, the truth is we don't know how it feels to die. Also not every patient will understand that it is ultimately assisted suicide, not a procedure. They would be the ones drinking the cocktail, injecting the drug, taking the pill, what have you. Finally, death always leaves more family struggles than we care to think about, even in the best cases. Families fighting over left assets and debts, struggling with your legacy and just what your death meant. This is all compounded in a suicide.

If all of those conditions are met then I could see it as my responsibility as a provider to create the conditions that would result in my patient's death.

TL;DR: Only if there's a consensus among a team of providers, the patient has requested it many times in a rational state, and the patient understands fully what they are about to do.
